report:
### Conclusion
Current clinical evidence indicates that while hypnosis may help certain individuals quit smoking, there is insufficient high-quality evidence to conclude that hypnotherapy is a consistently effective standalone treatment for smoking cessation.

### Key Evidence
- **Systematic Reviews**: The comprehensive Cochrane systematic review evaluated dozens of randomized controlled trials and found no clear evidence that hypnotherapy yields higher long-term quit rates than standard behavioral counseling, brief advice, or other interventions.
- **Inconsistent Clinical Findings**: Studies and meta-analyses show mixed results. Some individual trials report modest benefits—especially when hypnosis is paired with behavioral support—but small sample sizes and methodological differences prevent strong conclusions.
- **Clinical Role**: Medical organizations generally emphasize established first-line treatments with proven efficacy, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy and FDA-approved cessation medications (e.g., nicotine replacement therapy). Hypnosis is best viewed as a complementary tool that may support personal motivation rather than a proven primary solution.

### Sources
1. [Cochrane Evidence Review](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking)
2. [Frontiers in Psychology Meta-Analysis](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full)
3. [Healthline Medical Overview](https://www.healthline.com/health/hypnosis-to-quit-smoking)
4. [WebMD Hypnosis Guide](https://www.webmd.com/smoking-cessation/hypnosis-for-quitting-smoking)
